title: Release data
text: A reproducible ProtVis project should preserve more than final figures. At minimum, archive the quantitative matrix used for statistics, sample metadata, relevant protein annotations, differential/enrichment tables, parameter choices, process history, and a serialized ProtVis_dataset.

title: Release data
text: A reproducible ProtVis project should preserve more than final figures. At minimum, archive the quantitative matrix used for statistics, sample metadata, relevant protein annotations, differential/enrichment tables, parameter choices, process history, and a serialized ProtVis_dataset.

title: Release data
text:
Portable export
Programmatically, a complete project can be exported with:
export_dir <- export_protvis_dataset(
  dataset,
  directory = "ProtVis_release",
  include_raw = FALSE
)
The export contains ProtVis_dataset.rds, expression/sample/protein tables, annotation files, process history, stored analysis results, metadata JSON, and an HTML report. Set include_raw = TRUE when attached input files should also be copied and licensing/privacy rules permit it.

title: Release data
text:
Manuscript-ready package
For a publication, keep a simple hierarchy such as:
ProtVis_release/
  data/
  metadata/
  statistics/
  enrichment/
  figures/
  methods/
  ProtVis_dataset.rds
Do not use screenshots as the only copy of a quantitative result. Export the table behind every key figure.






Tip



Record the ProtVis package version and the date of the final analysis. For actively developed software, a commit SHA or tagged release improves reproducibility further.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text: The STRINGdb PPI toolkit connects a candidate protein list to known/predicted interaction evidence. It is most useful after DEP, enrichment, WGCNA or another analysis has already defined a biologically motivated candidate set.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text: The STRINGdb PPI toolkit connects a candidate protein list to known/predicted interaction evidence. It is most useful after DEP, enrichment, WGCNA or another analysis has already defined a biologically motivated candidate set.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
Recommended workflow

Prepare a clean candidate ID list.
Select the correct organism/species setting.
Map the identifiers to STRING-compatible IDs and review mapping success.
Build the interaction network using an appropriate confidence threshold.
Inspect disconnected proteins rather than silently dropping them.
Export the mapped identifiers, interaction table and final network figure.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
Interpretation
STRING integrates multiple evidence channels, and an edge does not necessarily indicate direct physical binding in your experimental system. Use the network to generate or organize hypotheses, then support key interactions with literature or experimental validation.

title: Protein links
text: Enter a gene identifier or UniProt accession. When a compatible identifier can be resolved, ProtVis provides direct links to resources such as UniProt, InterPro, and Swiss-Model.

title: Protein links
text: Enter a gene identifier or UniProt accession. When a compatible identifier can be resolved, ProtVis provides direct links to resources such as UniProt, InterPro, and Swiss-Model.

title: Protein links
text:
Sequence-based fallback
If an identifier is unavailable, the toolkit can use a protein sequence as a fallback and run local BLASTP against configured UniProt databases.
Local sequence search requires paths to:

a Swiss-Prot BLAST database;
a TrEMBL BLAST database;
the blastp executable.

The exact paths are machine-specific and should not be copied from another user’s computer.

title: Protein links
text:
Recommended workflow

Prefer a stable gene/UniProt identifier when available.
Use sequence-based BLAST only when ID mapping fails.
Review the best match, coverage and identity before accepting the mapping.
Open UniProt/InterPro/structure resources from the resolved accession.
Record the accession used in subsequent analysis.







Warning



The top BLAST hit is not automatically an ortholog or the biologically correct mapping. Check species, sequence coverage, identity, domain structure and database annotation before transferring functional interpretation.

title: DEG analyse
text: The DEG Analyse toolkit is separate from ProtVis’s main DEP analysis. Use the main DEP module for normalized protein-abundance comparisons. Use DEG Analyse only when the supplied dataset matches the statistical assumptions and input format expected by the toolkit.

title: DEG analyse
text: The DEG Analyse toolkit is separate from ProtVis’s main DEP analysis. Use the main DEP module for normalized protein-abundance comparisons. Use DEG Analyse only when the supplied dataset matches the statistical assumptions and input format expected by the toolkit.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Recommended workflow

Confirm whether the input represents raw counts, normalized continuous values, or another measurement type.
Provide the required sample grouping information.
Run the statistical model only after checking that its distributional assumptions match the input.
Inspect effect size, p-value and adjusted p-value together.
Export the full result table before thresholding.
State the model and threshold explicitly in downstream figures and Methods.







Important



Do not use an RNA-seq count model on continuous proteomics intensities merely because both datasets have samples in columns. Data type determines the appropriate statistical model.

title: Stacked column
text: The stacked-column utility is suited to composition-style data such as taxonomic categories, functional categories, pathway classes or other features whose contributions should be compared across samples.

title: Stacked column
text: The stacked-column utility is suited to composition-style data such as taxonomic categories, functional categories, pathway classes or other features whose contributions should be compared across samples.

title: Stacked column
text:
Recommended workflow

Prepare a table with explicit sample/group labels, category labels and numeric values.
Decide whether values should represent absolute abundance or proportions.
Aggregate rare categories into Other when a long legend would obscure the signal.
Generate the stacked-column plot.
Check that the category order and sample order support the biological comparison.
Export the underlying summarized table together with the figure.







Tip



For relative-abundance plots, verify that each sample sums to the intended denominator after filtering. Removing categories before renormalization changes the apparent proportions.

title: SwissModel
text:
The current SwissModel module accepts:

a protein sequence;
a Swiss-Model API token.

An example sequence can be inserted from the interface to verify the workflow.

title: SwissModel
text:
The current SwissModel module accepts:

a protein sequence;
a Swiss-Model API token.

An example sequence can be inserted from the interface to verify the workflow.

title: SwissModel
text:
Workflow

Paste the protein sequence.
Enter a valid API token.
Click Run.
Open the generated project link when available.
Review Project Information and the Model Quality table.
Inspect PDB Information, the Ramachandran Plot, Residue Composition, and the interactive 3D Structure.
Download the project information, PDB file and model-quality results.

title: SwissModel
text:
Interpretation
Model quality should be assessed before structural conclusions are drawn. Pay particular attention to template support, global/local quality estimates, unresolved/disordered regions and stereochemical diagnostics.






Warning



Do not publish or share API tokens in screenshots, notebooks, repositories or exported project files. Treat the token as a credential.

title: Protein extract
text: Upload a reference protein FASTA file and provide protein IDs either by pasting them line-by-line or by uploading a .txt, .csv, or .tsv list.

title: Protein extract
text: Upload a reference protein FASTA file and provide protein IDs either by pasting them line-by-line or by uploading a .txt, .csv, or .tsv list.

title: Protein extract
text:
Workflow

Upload the reference FASTA.
Enter or upload the target protein IDs.
Click Extract Proteins.
Review Matched Sequences, Sequence Table, FASTA Viewer, and Unmatched IDs.
Download the complete result package as a ZIP archive.

title: Protein extract
text:
Quality checks
Protein extraction is exact only when the ID syntax in the target list matches the FASTA headers. If many expected proteins are reported as unmatched, inspect whether the FASTA uses transcript suffixes, database prefixes, version suffixes, or pipe-delimited headers.






Tip



Keep the unmatched-ID list. It is useful for diagnosing annotation-version differences and prevents silent loss of candidates before downstream structure or enrichment analysis.

title: Correct noise
text:
The Correct Noise module loads the current ProtVis_dataset first. For older projects, it can fall back to Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda.
The interface has two explicit operations: Rename Columns and Correct Noise.

title: Correct noise
text:
The Correct Noise module loads the current ProtVis_dataset first. For older projects, it can fall back to Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda.
The interface has two explicit operations: Rename Columns and Correct Noise.

title: Correct noise
text:
Step 1: rename columns
ProtVis maps quantitative column names through the sample-information table, using maxquant_id to recover the intended sample_id when a mapping is available. If a matrix already uses valid sample IDs, those names are retained. Final names are made unique before downstream joins and reshaping.
This step is important because replicate grouping and later statistical comparisons depend on stable sample names.

title: Correct noise
text:
Step 2: correct noise
For datasets that use replicate suffixes _1, _2, and _3, ProtVis groups corresponding replicate columns and evaluates each protein within that group.

If at least two replicate measurements are non-zero, missing/zero cells are replaced using half of the sum of the non-zero replicate values.
If fewer than two non-zero replicates are present, the replicate-group values remain zero and are subsequently converted to NA.
If no recognizable replicate suffixes exist, ProtVis returns the validated matrix without applying replicate-level correction.
Duplicate protein IDs are collapsed before the correction step to prevent many-to-many joins from expanding the table.







Note



This behavior differs from the older cookbook description that referred to a generic “more than half missing” rule and mean imputation. The current source implements the replicate rule described above.

title: Correct noise
text:
GUI workflow

Click Load data.
Inspect Sample info and Expression Matrix.
Click Rename Columns and review the renamed table.
Click Correct Noise.
Inspect the corrected table before moving to transformation.

title: Correct noise
text:
Output
Results are saved into the active ProtVis_dataset. The compatibility stage file is:
Step3_correct_noise.rda
Continue with Data transformation.

title: Data imputation
text:
Proteomics missingness can arise from abundance limits, identification uncertainty, stochastic sampling, or technical failures. ProtVis therefore keeps missing values as NA until the user explicitly chooses an imputation method.
Before imputation, the current module coerces quantitative columns to numeric, converts non-finite values to missing, and handles not-observed sentinels such as 0 and -8 as NA.

title: Data imputation
text:
Proteomics missingness can arise from abundance limits, identification uncertainty, stochastic sampling, or technical failures. ProtVis therefore keeps missing values as NA until the user explicitly chooses an imputation method.
Before imputation, the current module coerces quantitative columns to numeric, converts non-finite values to missing, and handles not-observed sentinels such as 0 and -8 as NA.

title: Data imputation
text:
Available methods
The current GUI provides:







Method
Typical use




kNN
Local similarity-based imputation; current default


RF
Random-forest based imputation


Mean
Column/feature mean strategy, useful mainly as a simple baseline


Median
Robust central-value strategy


Zero
Explicit zero filling; use only when zero has a valid interpretation


Minimum
Low-value replacement strategy



Method choice should be justified by the expected missingness mechanism and downstream analysis.

title: Data imputation
text:
GUI workflow

Click Load data.
Click Visualize missing values before changing the matrix.
Inspect the original table and missingness visualization.
Select an imputation Method.
Click Run imputation.
Compare original and imputed distributions.
Download the diagnostic plots if they are part of the analysis record.







ImportantDefault does not mean universally correct



kNN is the interface default, but no imputation method is optimal for every proteomics design. Report the selected method in the Methods section of a manuscript and preserve the pre-imputation data for auditability.

title: Data imputation
text:
Output
The imputed state is stored in the active project object and in:
Step5_data_imputation.rda
Continue with Data normalization.

title: DEP analysis
text: The current DEP module uses limma (lmFit, contrasts, eBayes, topTable) on the normalized protein abundance matrix. Each row of the comparison table defines a Group1 versus Group2 contrast.

title: DEP analysis
text: The current DEP module uses limma (lmFit, contrasts, eBayes, topTable) on the normalized protein abundance matrix. Each row of the comparison table defines a Group1 versus Group2 contrast.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Prepare comparisons
ProtVis accepts a comparison table with exactly two columns:
Group1,Group2
Control,Treatment
Root,Shoot
You can upload .csv/.xlsx, paste a tab-delimited table, edit the built-in table, or use the demo comparison inferred from tissue/group metadata.
The group labels must exactly match values in the relevant sample_info grouping column.

title: DEP analysis
text:
GUI workflow

Click LOAD DATA.
Confirm Sample Info and Normalized Data.
Prepare the CompareGroup table.
Click RUN DEP.
Open each comparison tab to inspect the table, volcano plot, heatmap and DEP count summary.
Adjust the display/significance thresholds and export the final figures/tables.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Current significance controls
The volcano panel currently starts with:

logFC threshold = 0.27 (approximately a 1.21-fold change on a log2 scale);
P-value threshold = 0.05.

The displayed regulation classification uses logFC together with the raw limma P.Value. The limma result table also contains multiple-testing-adjusted statistics.






ImportantFor publication-grade inference



If your analysis plan requires FDR control, base the final biological claims and downstream ID list on the adjusted p-value column (for example adj.P.Val) rather than assuming the volcano panel’s raw P.Value threshold is an FDR threshold. Record the exact thresholds used in the manuscript Methods.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Dynamic plots
Volcano thresholds are reactive: changing them reclassifies proteins and keeps the DEP heatmap synchronized with the currently significant set. Heatmaps sanitize non-finite values only for plotting; this does not rewrite the differential-statistics table.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Output and downstream handoff
DEP results are attached to the active project object and are available to Enrichment analysis. The current enrichment loader checks the project object first and can also recover differential results from:
Step7_differential_analysis.rda
with older filenames retained only as migration fallbacks.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Use Overview before differential abundance analysis. It is the fastest way to catch sample swaps, strong batch effects, failed replicates, unexpected missingness, and normalization problems.
The current module can load both the imputed and normalized stages. When stage snapshots are unavailable but a valid ProtVis_dataset is active, ProtVis derives an imputed/centered overview from the current object and reports that fallback.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Use Overview before differential abundance analysis. It is the fastest way to catch sample swaps, strong batch effects, failed replicates, unexpected missingness, and normalization problems.
The current module can load both the imputed and normalized stages. When stage snapshots are unavailable but a valid ProtVis_dataset is active, ProtVis derives an imputed/centered overview from the current object and reports that fallback.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Correlation
Choose Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall correlation, then configure clustering and whether correlation values/sample names are displayed. Use this panel to check whether biological replicates are more similar to each other than to unrelated groups.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Expression pattern
The expression-pattern heatmap can focus on the top variable features and optionally scale by protein or sample. This is useful for a global view of coordinated abundance patterns, not as a replacement for formal differential testing.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Dimensionality reduction
Available methods are:

PCA
PCoA
t-SNE
UMAP
NMDS

Color/ellipse grouping can use group, tissue, species, batch, or condition; point shape can be assigned independently. The default DR view uses tissue for color/95% confidence ellipses and species for point shape when those fields are available.
ProtVis displays dimensionality reduction before normalization and after normalization, enabling direct assessment of how preprocessing changed sample structure.

title: Overview & QC
Overview & QC
text:
What to look for
A healthy dataset does not need every replicate to overlap perfectly. Instead, look for consistency with the experimental design: replicate proximity, plausible separation of known groups, no isolated failed sample, comparable post-normalization distributions, and missingness that can be biologically/technically explained.






Warning



A visually attractive PCA is not proof that preprocessing is correct. If normalization creates a separation that contradicts known biology or removes a strong expected effect, revisit the preceding stages.

title: Pathview
text:
The current Pathview module uses two CSV files.


Two columns:
KO,logFC
K00844,1.25
K01810,-0.83
KO identifiers are normalized to the Kxxxxx format.



Three columns:
pathway,ko,Description
map00010,K00844,Glycolysis / Gluconeogenesis

title: Pathview
text:
GUI workflow

Upload the KO/logFC file.
Upload the pathway-to-KO annotation file.
Choose Plant, Animals, Bacteria, Fungi, Eukaryotes, or Hsa.
Click Run KEGG Enrichment.
Select an enriched pathway.
Click Draw Selected Pathway.

ProtVis filters to valid KO identifiers, performs enrichment, then calls pathview with species = "ko" and native KEGG output. Multiple KO values mapping to the same node are summarized by the mean.

title: Pathview
text:
Output
The native KEGG pathway is written as a PNG in the current working directory and shown in the interface together with a KO/logFC preview.






NoteInternet access may be required



Pathview can require access to KEGG resources while generating the native pathway map. If enrichment succeeds but no PNG is generated, verify the KO IDs, selected pathway and network access.

title: Installation
text:
ProtVis is an R package with a Shiny interface. Use a recent R installation and a writable R library. On Windows, installing packages from source may also require the matching Rtools release when a binary is unavailable.






Note



This cookbook currently follows ProtVis 0.5.7 on the dev branch. The installation commands below therefore install @dev explicitly.

title: Installation
text:
ProtVis is an R package with a Shiny interface. Use a recent R installation and a writable R library. On Windows, installing packages from source may also require the matching Rtools release when a binary is unavailable.






Note



This cookbook currently follows ProtVis 0.5.7 on the dev branch. The installation commands below therefore install @dev explicitly.

title: Installation
text:
Recommended installation
Install pak once, then install ProtVis from GitHub:
options(repos = c(
  CRAN = "https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/CRAN/"
))

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("xuebinzhang-lab/ProtVis@dev")
Verify the installed version:
packageVersion("ProtVis")

title: Installation
text:
Clean update
When an old installation is stale, locked, or its lazy-load database is corrupted, use the clean installer supplied by ProtVis:
source(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuebinzhang-lab/ProtVis/dev/install_ProtVis.R"
)
Close other R sessions that are currently using ProtVis before running a clean reinstall.

title: Installation
text:
Optional WGCNA helper
Some WGCNA workflows may use the optional helper package documented by ProtVis:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ShawnWx2019/WGCNAShinyFun", ref = "master")
You do not need this optional dependency to launch the core application.

title: Installation
text:
Launch ProtVis
library(ProtVis)
run_ProtVis()
or directly:
ProtVis::run_ProtVis()

title: Installation
text:
First launch checklist
After the application opens, confirm that you can see Homepage, Project init, Data input, Pre-processing, Downstream analysis, Multi-omics, PTM, Release data, Toolkits, and Help in the navigation bar.
If the app opens but an optional module reports a missing dependency, install that dependency and restart the R session. If the package itself fails to load after an update, prefer the clean installer above rather than repeatedly installing over a corrupted package directory.

title: Project init
text: Project init establishes the analysis context shared by all later modules. It defines the output directory, sample metadata, quantitative expression data, and source type, then validates them and creates the first ProtVis_dataset.

title: Project init
text: Project init establishes the analysis context shared by all later modules. It defines the output directory, sample metadata, quantitative expression data, and source type, then validates them and creates the first ProtVis_dataset.

title: Project init
text:
Inputs
The current interface accepts sample information and an expression matrix in .csv, .xlsx, or .xls format. It also provides bundled source-specific examples that can be loaded directly from the package.
A practical sample-information table contains at least a unique sample identifier and experimental grouping information. ProtVis commonly uses the following fields when available:







Column
Purpose




sample_id
Unique sample name used by downstream matrices and plots


maxquant_id
Original source/export name used when sample columns must be mapped or renamed


group
Experimental group used for comparisons


tissue
Optional biological tissue; used by several demo and DR workflows


species
Optional species grouping or point-shape metadata


batch
Optional batch grouping


condition
Optional condition grouping



The expression matrix should contain a protein identifier plus numeric sample columns. Sample columns must be unambiguously alignable to sample_info.

title: Project init
text:
Supported source selections
The current Project init menu includes Raw, MaxQuant, ProteomeDiscoverer / Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, Mascot, OpenMS, and User-defined matrix.

title: Project init
text:
GUI workflow

Click Set working directory and choose a writable project directory.
Upload Sample Information and inspect the preview.
Upload the Expression Matrix, or select a Built-in example and click Load selected built-in example.
Choose the matching Data source.
Confirm that sample information and expression-matrix previews are correct.
Click Project init.

ProtVis validates the sample/matrix relationship before creating the project object. A successful initialization also triggers an automatic portable export.

title: Project init
text:
Outputs
The primary output is a validated ProtVis_dataset stored in the shared project state. The object receives a traceable name such as:
ProtVis_dataset__project_init__maxquant__v1
For compatibility with the stage-oriented workflow, ProtVis also writes:
Step1_project_init.rda
The stage file contains one ProtVis_dataset, rather than separate unrelated workspace variables.






TipUse the built-in examples first



If you are testing a fresh installation, load one of the bundled examples. This verifies Project init, sample alignment, source parsing, and output-directory permissions before you introduce your own data.

title: Project init
text:
Common validation problems
Sample names do not match. Check sample_id, maxquant_id, and expression-matrix column names. Do not silently reorder samples outside ProtVis without recording the change.
Duplicate protein IDs. Resolve duplicated identifiers before downstream statistics when the biological meaning of the duplicates is ambiguous. Source parsers may apply source-specific collapsing rules, but a user-defined matrix should be explicit.
Working directory cannot be selected. Choose a local directory you can write to. ProtVis normalizes the selected path and rejects inaccessible directories instead of proceeding with an invalid project location.

title: PTM analysis
text:
The PTM section is intended for modification-centric proteomics workflows in which peptide/site-level evidence needs to be inspected separately from ordinary protein abundance analysis.
Because PTM search-engine exports differ substantially in site localization, peptide sequence, modification notation and protein mapping, always check that the selected source parser and input columns match the dataset that generated the evidence.

title: PTM analysis
text:
The PTM section is intended for modification-centric proteomics workflows in which peptide/site-level evidence needs to be inspected separately from ordinary protein abundance analysis.
Because PTM search-engine exports differ substantially in site localization, peptide sequence, modification notation and protein mapping, always check that the selected source parser and input columns match the dataset that generated the evidence.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Recommended workflow

Complete the standard project setup and source selection.
Open PTM and load the PTM-specific table expected by the module.
Verify modified sequence/site notation and protein identifiers before filtering.
Apply localization/evidence filters appropriate to the experiment.
Inspect modification-level quantitative patterns separately from total protein abundance.
Export the filtered evidence table used for every figure.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Biological interpretation
A change at a phosphosite, acetylation site or other PTM can reflect altered modification occupancy, altered total protein abundance, or both. When possible, compare PTM abundance with the corresponding protein-level signal before assigning a regulatory interpretation.






Warning



Do not interpret a modified peptide as a unique site when the search result does not localize the modification confidently. Preserve the original localization evidence in the exported record.

title: Co-enrichment
text: Co-enrichment is useful when several contrasts, omics layers, tissues, or protein clusters have already been analyzed and you want to distinguish shared functional themes from condition-specific terms.

title: Co-enrichment
text: Co-enrichment is useful when several contrasts, omics layers, tissues, or protein clusters have already been analyzed and you want to distinguish shared functional themes from condition-specific terms.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Recommended inputs
Use enrichment result sets derived from compatible identifier/background systems. If two analyses used different gene universes or incompatible annotation versions, direct comparison of p-values can be misleading.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Workflow

Generate the individual enrichment results first.
Standardize term identifiers and term descriptions.
Select the result sets to compare.
Run the co-enrichment module.
Inspect shared and unique terms and their direction/strength where the module provides those metrics.
Export the underlying comparison table rather than relying only on the figure.







Tip



For cross-experiment comparisons, term IDs are more reliable join keys than descriptions because descriptions can change between database versions.

title: Metaproteomics
text:
The current metaproteomics module joins three CSV tables by ProteinID.


ProteinID,Control_1,Control_2,Treatment_1,Treatment_2
P001,100,120,160,150



Required columns:
ProteinID,Phylum,Genus,Species



Required columns:
ProteinID,KO,Pathway,COG
A built-in demo and downloadable demo tables are provided in the interface.

title: Metaproteomics
text:
The current metaproteomics module joins three CSV tables by ProteinID.


ProteinID,Control_1,Control_2,Treatment_1,Treatment_2
P001,100,120,160,150



Required columns:
ProteinID,Phylum,Genus,Species



Required columns:
ProteinID,KO,Pathway,COG
A built-in demo and downloadable demo tables are provided in the interface.

title: Metaproteomics
text:
Analysis settings
Choose a taxonomic level (Phylum, Genus, Species) and a functional level (Pathway, KO, COG). You can switch between summed intensity and relative abundance and choose how many top categories are displayed.

title: Metaproteomics
Metaproteomics
text:
Group labels
In the current module, sample names containing terms such as treat, case, or disease are assigned to Treatment; other samples default to Control for the display grouping. Use clear sample names when relying on this behavior.






Important



Taxonomic and functional annotations can be many-to-many in real metaproteomes. Confirm how protein groups, shared peptides and ambiguous taxonomic assignments were handled upstream before interpreting summed compositions as organism-level abundance.

title: Expression profile
text: Expression-profile analysis is useful when the main question is not a single pairwise difference but a pattern across several samples, stages, tissues or conditions. Proteins with similar trajectories can be grouped into trend clusters and interpreted together.

title: Expression profile
text: Expression-profile analysis is useful when the main question is not a single pairwise difference but a pattern across several samples, stages, tissues or conditions. Proteins with similar trajectories can be grouped into trend clusters and interpreted together.

title: Expression profile
text:
Recommended input
Use a normalized protein abundance matrix with stable protein IDs and samples in the intended biological order. If samples represent an ordered series, arrange them chronologically or biologically before clustering so the trend plot is interpretable.

title: Expression profile
text:
Workflow

Load or upload the quantitative expression matrix required by the module.
Confirm sample order and protein identifiers.
Choose the clustering settings and number of clusters/centers.
Run the expression-profile analysis.
Inspect whether clusters represent stable, increasing, decreasing, transient or condition-specific patterns.
Export cluster membership before using cluster IDs for enrichment or network analysis.

title: Expression profile
text:
Interpretation
Choose the number of clusters based on stability and biological interpretability rather than visual preference alone. Very large K values can split one coherent pattern into many small groups, whereas very small K values can merge distinct biological responses.






Note



Trend clustering is exploratory. A cluster does not by itself establish statistical significance for every protein it contains; use appropriate differential or time-series statistics when formal inference is required.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text: ProtVis defines an ordered analysis progression from creation/import through preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, differential analysis, enrichment, and network analysis. Checkpoints capture a validated ProtVis_dataset at a named stage.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text: ProtVis defines an ordered analysis progression from creation/import through preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, differential analysis, enrichment, and network analysis. Checkpoints capture a validated ProtVis_dataset at a named stage.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Save a checkpoint
checkpoint <- save_protvis_checkpoint(
  dataset = ds,
  directory = "checkpoints",
  stage = "normalization",
  keep = 20
)

checkpoint
Checkpoint files use names beginning with:
protvis_checkpoint_<stage>_...rds
Saving is validated before a checkpoint is published, reducing the chance that a partial write replaces a usable analysis state.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
List checkpoints
list_protvis_checkpoints("checkpoints")
The returned table includes the file path, stage, creation time, size, MD5, and whether the checkpoint can be read.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Restore the newest checkpoint
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  version = "latest"
)
You can request a stage as well:
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  stage = "differential_analysis"
)
If the exact requested stage is unavailable, ProtVis can select the newest readable checkpoint at or before that stage, allowing an interrupted workflow to resume from the closest valid state.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Automatic persistence
Many GUI stages persist the active object automatically. protvis_auto_export_dataset() writes a portable export bundle and records the latest output location in the dataset metadata.
ds <- protvis_auto_export_dataset(
  ds,
  directory = getwd(),
  include_raw = FALSE
)

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Legacy stage files
ProtVis still reads historical stage files where needed. Current stage snapshots are written with exactly one ProtVis_dataset object; older workspaces that stored expression and sample objects separately can be migrated by the internal loading layer.
Common compatibility files include:
Step1_project_init.rda
Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda
Step3_correct_noise.rda
Step4_data_transformed.rda
Step5_data_imputation.rda
Step6_data_normalization.rda
Step7_differential_analysis.rda






TipRecovery strategy



For long projects, keep the working directory together with the latest portable export and checkpoint directory. This gives you a human-readable export, a complete serialized project object, and stage-aware recovery options.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
ProtVis combines data import, preprocessing, quality control, statistical analysis, functional interpretation, multi-omics integration, PTM analysis, and publication-ready visualization in one interactive workflow. This cookbook follows the application in the same order that a real project is analyzed.
Start with installation · Understand ProtVis_dataset · Run the full workflow

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
ProtVis combines data import, preprocessing, quality control, statistical analysis, functional interpretation, multi-omics integration, PTM analysis, and publication-ready visualization in one interactive workflow. This cookbook follows the application in the same order that a real project is analyzed.
Start with installation · Understand ProtVis_dataset · Run the full workflow

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
Recommended analysis path

Install and launch ProtVis.
Project init: choose the working directory, load sample metadata and an expression matrix or built-in example, then select the data source.
Data input: parse and validate the source-specific quantitative evidence.
Pre-processing: Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization.
Overview: inspect sample correlations, expression patterns, dimensionality reduction, missingness, intensity distributions, PCA, and CV.
DEP: define one or more Group1 versus Group2 comparisons and run differential abundance analysis.
Interpretation: use GO/KEGG enrichment, GSEA, Pathview, PPI, WGCNA, and other downstream modules as appropriate.
Release/export: save portable project outputs and publication-ready tables and figures.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
Two ways to learn ProtVis
GUI-first users can follow the chapter order in the sidebar. Each page explains prerequisites, the controls to use, expected outputs, and common failure points.
Reproducible-workflow users should also read ProtVis_dataset and Checkpoints & recovery. These chapters explain how ProtVis preserves analysis provenance and how projects can be resumed without rebuilding every previous step.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
ProtVis_dataset is an independent S4 class designed for proteomics. It does not inherit from mass_dataset and does not require the massdataset package. Its validity checks enforce exact alignment between expression columns and sample_info, and between expression rows and variable_info.
This architecture allows ProtVis to preserve one coherent scientific record while every module adds a new result or processing step.

text:

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Core components







Component
What it stores




expression_data
Numeric protein-by-sample abundance matrix


sample_info
Sample identifiers and experimental metadata


variable_info
Protein/feature metadata aligned to expression rows


annotation
Fixed annotation schema with eggnog_output, GO_annotation, and KEGG_annotation


analysis_results
Stage-specific statistical and biological results


process_info
Active stage, parameters, messages, status and history


metadata
Project-level information, source and object naming/version information


other_files
Imported-file provenance and stored auxiliary resources


checkpoint_info
Checkpoint/recovery and export metadata



The historical names annotation_table and ms2_data are not part of the current annotation model.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Create a dataset programmatically
library(ProtVis)

expr <- data.frame(
  S1 = c(10, 20, 30),
  S2 = c(12, 18, 33),
  row.names = c("P1", "P2", "P3")
)

samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S1", "S2"),
  group = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  row.names = c("S1", "S2")
)

ds <- create_protvis_dataset(
  expression_data = expr,
  sample_info = samples,
  metadata = list(source = "User-defined matrix")
)

validate_protvis_dataset(ds)
For day-to-day GUI use, Project init creates this object automatically.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Inspect a built-in project
library(ProtVis)

ds <- load_protvis_builtin_data(
  source = "DIA-NN",
  auto_export = FALSE
)

class(ds)
slotNames(ds)
dim(ds$expression_data)
head(ds$sample_info)
Use protvis_expression_matrix(ds) when you need an ID-first data frame suitable for UI boundaries or export.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Object versions
ProtVis analysis helpers create traceable object versions rather than overwriting an unnamed global object. Object names encode the project stage or method, for example transformation or differential-analysis versions. The object retains parameters and process history so results can be related back to their analytical context.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Annotation schema
The annotation slot always exposes the same three named data frames:
names(ds$annotation)
# eggnog_output, GO_annotation, KEGG_annotation
Missing annotation layers are represented as empty data frames rather than changing the object schema. This makes downstream code more predictable.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Export a portable project
out <- export_protvis_dataset(
  ds,
  directory = "ProtVis_export",
  include_raw = FALSE
)

out
The export bundle contains the serialized ProtVis_dataset, expression and metadata tables, annotation tables, process history, serialized analysis results, a metadata JSON file, and an HTML report. If include_raw = TRUE, available attached source files are also copied.






ImportantTreat the object as the authoritative record



Stage .rda files are useful for compatibility and recovery, but new analyses should use the active ProtVis_dataset whenever possible. This prevents parameter, annotation, and provenance information from becoming detached from the quantitative matrix.

title: Multi-omics
text:
The Multi-omics menu groups analyses that extend beyond a single DEP table:







Module
Main question




Expression Profile
Which proteins share similar abundance trends?


WGCNA
Which co-expression modules and hub proteins relate to traits?


Metaproteomics
How do taxonomic and functional compositions change together?


Nine Quadrant
How do two quantitative contrasts/datasets agree or disagree?


Co-enrichment
Which functional signals are shared or distinct across result sets?


Venn
Which identifiers overlap among multiple sets?



These modules do not all require the same input type. Follow the dedicated page for each analysis rather than assuming the normalized matrix alone is sufficient.






Tip



For manuscript figures, use an integration module only when the biological question is genuinely cross-layer or network-oriented. A more complex plot is not automatically more informative than a well-supported DEP or enrichment result.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
Input
Upload a .txt, .tsv, or .csv expression matrix. The first column should contain feature IDs and the remaining columns should be samples. The format selector includes count, expected count, normalized count, peak area (metabolomics), and protein abundance.
Select an unsigned or signed network and the appropriate preprocessing/normalization mode for the supplied data.

title: WGCNA
text:
Filtering
The first filter removes low-abundance features based on sample percentage and expression cutoff. The second filter ranks variability using MAD or Variance and retains the requested number of features.
Filtering is especially important for proteomics because a network built from thousands of uninformative or extremely sparse proteins can be unstable and computationally expensive.

title: WGCNA
text:
Soft-threshold selection
Run the soft-threshold analysis, review the scale-free topology fit, and either use the recommended power or specify a justified custom power. The default target displayed by the UI is an \(R^2\) cutoff of 0.8.

title: WGCNA
text:
Module detection
Set minimum module size, module merge/cut-tree height, and maximum block size, then run module detection. Export the protein-to-module table so every downstream claim can be traced back to module membership.

title: WGCNA
text:
Trait association
Upload trait data and run module-trait analysis. Check sample names carefully: trait rows/columns must correspond to the same samples represented in the expression matrix.

title: WGCNA
text:
Hub proteins and Cytoscape
Select a trait and module, set absolute kME/GS cutoffs, and run hub analysis. ProtVis can generate node and edge tables for Cytoscape using a user-defined network-weight threshold.






Warning



WGCNA requires enough samples to estimate correlations meaningfully. Very small proteomics experiments can produce visually convincing but unstable networks. Treat network topology cautiously when sample size is limited.

title: Nine quadrant
text: A nine-quadrant plot compares two effect estimates, usually log fold changes from matched contrasts. Thresholds on the x and y axes divide proteins/features into combinations such as concordant increase, concordant decrease, discordant response, or weak/no change.

title: Nine quadrant
text: A nine-quadrant plot compares two effect estimates, usually log fold changes from matched contrasts. Thresholds on the x and y axes divide proteins/features into combinations such as concordant increase, concordant decrease, discordant response, or weak/no change.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Recommended workflow

Prepare two result tables that share a stable feature identifier.
Confirm that both effect columns use the same direction convention (for example Treatment minus Control).
Merge only on the intended identifier.
Set biologically/statistically justified x- and y-axis thresholds.
Inspect concordant and discordant quadrants separately.
Export the merged classification table together with the plot.







Warning



If one contrast is A - B and the other is B - A, the apparent concordance will be reversed. Always verify contrast direction before interpreting quadrants.

title: Venn
text: Venn diagrams are useful for a small number of clearly defined ID sets, such as significant proteins from two or three contrasts. They are not ideal for many sets; use an UpSet-style approach outside the module when intersections become difficult to read.

title: Venn
text: Venn diagrams are useful for a small number of clearly defined ID sets, such as significant proteins from two or three contrasts. They are not ideal for many sets; use an UpSet-style approach outside the module when intersections become difficult to read.

title: Venn
text:
Workflow

Prepare each set using the same identifier namespace.
Remove empty IDs and accidental duplicates within each set.
Load the sets into the Venn module.
Confirm set names and intersection counts.
Export both the figure and, when needed, the IDs belonging to biologically important intersections.







Note



An overlap count is descriptive. Whether the overlap is more than expected by chance requires an explicit statistical test and a defined background universe.

title: PD strict spectrum
text: PD Strict Spectrum provides a dedicated route for Proteome Discoverer evidence that needs stricter spectrum-level inspection than a protein-level abundance table can provide.

title: PD strict spectrum
text: PD Strict Spectrum provides a dedicated route for Proteome Discoverer evidence that needs stricter spectrum-level inspection than a protein-level abundance table can provide.

title: PD strict spectrum
text:
Workflow principles

Use the original Proteome Discoverer export expected by the module.
Confirm peptide sequence, modification/site annotation, spectrum identifiers and score/evidence fields before applying filters.
Retain the unfiltered source file and export the exact filtered subset used for interpretation.
For candidate PTM sites used in a manuscript, manually inspect the relevant fragmentation/localization evidence when possible.







Note



Spectrum-level validation supports identification confidence; it does not replace quantitative replication or statistical testing across biological samples.

title: Overview
text:
ProtVis is an interactive R/Shiny platform for proteomics and metaproteomics processing, statistical analysis, biological interpretation, and scientific visualization. The current application is organized around a reproducible project object, ProtVis_dataset, so quantitative data, metadata, annotations, analysis results, imported files, and processing history remain connected throughout the workflow.
ProtVis is designed for researchers who want a GUI without giving up traceability. Most analysis modules can be used interactively, while the underlying package also exposes functions for importing data, validating projects, running pipelines, saving checkpoints, and exporting complete analysis bundles.

text:

The current application is organized around a reproducible project object, ProtVis_dataset, so quantitative data, metadata, annotations, analysis results, imported files, and processing history remain connected throughout the workflow.

title: Overview
text:
Current analytical scope







Stage
Main capabilities




Project setup
Working directory, sample information, expression matrix, built-in examples, source selection


Data input
MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, Mascot, OpenMS, Raw, user-defined matrices


Pre-processing
Replicate-aware noise correction, transformation, missing-value inspection and imputation, median-centering normalization


Overview/QC
Correlation, expression-pattern heatmap, PCA, PCoA, t-SNE, UMAP, NMDS, total intensity, missingness, distributions, CV


Differential abundance

Functional interpretation
GO/KEGG enrichment, GSEA, Pathview, STRINGdb PPI


Multi-omics
Expression profile, WGCNA, metaproteomics, nine quadrant, co-enrichment, Venn


PTM and evidence
PTM analysis and Proteome Discoverer strict-spectrum inspection


Toolkits
Protein extraction, background construction, external protein links, protein structure, SwissModel, boxplots, correlation chord and other utilities

title: Overview
text:
The key architectural change: ProtVis_dataset
Earlier ProtVis workflows were described primarily as a chain of .rda files. Current ProtVis keeps those stage files for compatibility and recovery, but the canonical representation is now a validated ProtVis_dataset object.
A project object keeps the protein-by-sample expression matrix aligned with sample and protein metadata, stores fixed annotation layers (eggnog_output, GO_annotation, and KEGG_annotation), records analysis results, and captures process history and checkpoint information. See ProtVis_dataset for the full model.






ImportantWhy this matters



A result should not be separated from the data and parameters that produced it. ProtVis therefore creates new traceable object versions as analysis proceeds instead of treating each plot as an isolated end product.

title: Overview
text:
Recommended order
For a standard quantitative proteomics project, use:
Project init → Data input → Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization → Overview → DEP analysis → Enrichment/GSEA/Pathview
Then add WGCNA, PPI, co-enrichment, metaproteomics, PTM, or other specialized modules when they address the biological question.

title: Overview
section: What is reproducible and what is interactive?
text:
What is reproducible and what is interactive?
The GUI is intended for interactive exploration, parameter selection, and figure export. Reproducibility is supported by the persisted ProtVis_dataset, stage snapshots, process history, checkpoints, and portable exports. For analyses that need scripted automation, use package-level functions such as load_protvis_builtin_data(), create_protvis_dataset(), run_protvis_pipeline(), save_protvis_checkpoint(), and export_protvis_dataset().

title: GSEA
text:
The current GSEA module is a file-driven workflow. It reads an expression/count matrix, group information, and KO-to-pathway annotation, calculates a DESeq2 ranking, and passes the ranked log2 fold changes to clusterProfiler::GSEA().
Because the ranking step uses DESeq2, the uploaded matrix must be appropriate for DESeq2 count modeling. Do not upload already log-transformed continuous protein intensities and assume they are equivalent to counts.

title: GSEA
text:
The current GSEA module is a file-driven workflow. It reads an expression/count matrix, group information, and KO-to-pathway annotation, calculates a DESeq2 ranking, and passes the ranked log2 fold changes to clusterProfiler::GSEA().
Because the ranking step uses DESeq2, the uploaded matrix must be appropriate for DESeq2 count modeling. Do not upload already log-transformed continuous protein intensities and assume they are equivalent to counts.

title: GSEA
text:
Required files

Expression matrix (.txt)
First column: ID. Remaining columns: samples.
ID   S1   S2   S3   S4
K00001  120  130  240  220
K00002   40   35   70   65


Group information (.txt)
Required columns:
Sample   Group
S1       Control
S2       Control
S3       Treatment
S4       Treatment


KO pathway information (.txt)
The current parser uses the first column as pathway/term ID and the third column as a semicolon-separated gene/KO list.

title: GSEA
text:
GUI workflow

Upload the Expression Matrix.
Upload Group Info.
Upload KO Pathway Info.
Set minGSSize and maxGSSize.
Set the number of top pathways to display.
Optionally show only p.adjust < 0.05 results.
Sort the dotplot by absolute NES or by p.adjust.
Click Run Analysis.
Select a pathway to inspect its enrichment curve.

title: GSEA
Enrichment analysis
text:
Enrichment analysis uses two components:

a gene/protein ID list;
an Enrichment Analysis File containing the GO and KEGG background definitions.



The current module follows this priority:

an uploaded gene-list file (.csv or .xlsx);
IDs pasted in manual mode;
significant IDs from the selected DEP comparison.

Uploaded/pasted gene-list data should contain an ID column. The parser also recognizes common variants such as gene/protein ID names, but using ID is the most portable choice.



Upload one .xlsx workbook with both worksheets:
GO_background
KEGG_background
Each worksheet must contain:
TERM   GENE   NAME
TERM is the ontology/pathway identifier, GENE contains associated IDs (multiple IDs can be separated by common delimiters), and NAME is the human-readable term name.
After clicking Check File, ProtVis previews the first rows of both sheets. A validated workbook is stored with the active ProtVis_dataset; when it is selected before Project init, ProtVis retains it and attaches it when the project object is created.

title: Enrichment analysis
text:
Run the analysis

Open Enrichment analysis.
Click LOAD DATA if you want to choose among stored DEP comparisons.
Upload and Check File for the enrichment workbook.
Either upload/paste an ID list or allow ProtVis to use the selected DEP list automatically.
Choose the taxonomic group: Plant, Animals, Bacteria, Fungi, Eukaryotes, or Hsa.
Select GO, KEGG, or both.
Click Analysis.

title: Enrichment analysis
text:
Results and plots
GO and KEGG each provide a result table and visualization. Available plot types are Bar plot, Dot plot, and Circle plot. You can choose the number of top terms, change presentation colors, download the plot as PDF, and export the result table as CSV.






TipWhen the plot is empty but the table is valid



Check whether any term passes the plotting significance/filter criteria and whether the uploaded IDs use the same identifier namespace as the background GENE column. Identifier mismatch is a common reason for zero overlap.

title: Enrichment analysis
text:
Reproducibility
The enrichment workbook is not treated as a disposable upload. Both validated background sheets are retained in the project object’s provenance/auxiliary-file layer so the analysis can be reopened without reconstructing the original workbook manually.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
The standard downstream workflow begins after Data Normalization. ProtVis then provides two complementary views of the data:

Overview asks whether the dataset is technically and biologically coherent.
DEP analysis asks which proteins differ between defined groups.

Functional modules such as enrichment, GSEA, Pathview and PPI should be interpreted in the context of those upstream checks.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
The standard downstream workflow begins after Data Normalization. ProtVis then provides two complementary views of the data:

Overview asks whether the dataset is technically and biologically coherent.
DEP analysis asks which proteins differ between defined groups.

Functional modules such as enrichment, GSEA, Pathview and PPI should be interpreted in the context of those upstream checks.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Recommended order

Overview & QC — inspect correlations, distributions, missingness, PCA/CV and dimensionality-reduction structure.
DEP analysis — run one or more explicit Group1 versus Group2 comparisons.
Enrichment analysis — test significant protein IDs against GO/KEGG backgrounds.
GSEA — use a ranked signal when a thresholded DEP list would discard useful pathway-level information.
Pathview — project KO-level log fold changes onto a selected KEGG pathway.
Add STRINGdb PPI, WGCNA, co-enrichment or other network/integration modules when relevant.







ImportantSeparate statistical evidence from visualization settings



Changing colors, point sizes, heatmap labels or plot dimensions should not change the underlying statistical model. In contrast, changing a fold-change or p-value threshold changes which proteins are labeled significant and therefore affects heatmaps and downstream gene lists.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Canonical data flow
Current modules prefer the active ProtVis_dataset. Compatibility stage files remain readable when a project is reopened. Downstream results are stored in analysis_results and process history so the quantitative matrix and derived statistics stay connected.

title: Data normalization
text:
The current ProtVis normalization module performs median subtraction. For each numeric sample column, ProtVis subtracts that column’s median (ignoring NA values):
\[x'_{ij} = x_{ij} - \operatorname{median}(x_{\cdot j})\]
After normalization, each sample is centered around a comparable median while relative within-sample differences are retained.

title: Data normalization
text:
The current ProtVis normalization module performs median subtraction. For each numeric sample column, ProtVis subtracts that column’s median (ignoring NA values):
\[x'_{ij} = x_{ij} - \operatorname{median}(x_{\cdot j})\]
After normalization, each sample is centered around a comparable median while relative within-sample differences are retained.

title: Data normalization
text:
GUI workflow

Click Load data. The module uses the imputed ProtVis_dataset/Step5_data_imputation.rda.
Inspect the original data and boxplot.
Click Run normalization.
Compare the normalized data and boxplot with the input.
Adjust display colors if desired.
Download the original and normalized PDF plots for reporting.

title: Data normalization
text:
Interpretation
Median subtraction is useful when broad sample-level offsets are considered technical rather than biological. It is not appropriate to assume this for every experimental design. If most proteins are expected to shift globally in one direction for biological reasons, inspect the distributions carefully before interpreting normalized fold changes.

title: Data normalization
text:
Output
The normalized project state is persisted as a ProtVis_dataset and as:
Step6_data_normalization.rda
This stage is the standard input for Overview and DEP analysis.






Tip



Before differential abundance analysis, open Overview and check sample total intensity, missingness, intensity distributions, PCA, CV, and group structure. Normalization should improve technical comparability without destroying the expected experimental pattern.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
ProtVis separates preprocessing into four explicit modules:
Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization
Keeping these decisions separate makes it easier to inspect the effect of each operation and to record the selected method in the project history.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
ProtVis separates preprocessing into four explicit modules:
Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization
Keeping these decisions separate makes it easier to inspect the effect of each operation and to record the selected method in the project history.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
1. Correct noise
The current noise-correction logic is replicate-aware. For sample groups whose names contain replicate suffixes such as _1, _2, and _3, zero/missing cells are corrected only when sufficient non-zero replicate evidence exists; otherwise the affected replicate group remains missing. Duplicate protein IDs are collapsed safely before reshaping to avoid accidental many-to-many expansion.
Read Correct noise.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
2. Data transformation
ProtVis currently exposes None, log10, log2, Standardization, Z-Score, scale, center, and scale-center. Original and transformed distributions can be compared before proceeding.
Read Data transformation.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
3. Data imputation
Missing measurements are visualized before imputation. The current GUI offers kNN, RF, Mean, Median, Zero, and Minimum, with kNN selected by default. Legacy missing sentinels such as 0 and -8 are kept as true NA until the user runs imputation.
Read Data imputation.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
4. Data normalization
The current normalization module performs column-wise median subtraction, centering each sample by its median. Original and normalized boxplots can be compared and downloaded.
Read Data normalization.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
Stage outputs
The canonical result after each step is a new ProtVis_dataset state. Compatibility stage files are also used by the GUI:



Stage
Compatibility file




Correct noise
Step3_correct_noise.rda


Transformation
Step4_data_transformed.rda


Imputation
Step5_data_imputation.rda


Normalization
Step6_data_normalization.rda









WarningDo not impute before inspecting missingness



Missing values in proteomics are not always random. Use the missing-value visualization and the biological design to decide whether a global imputation strategy is appropriate for your experiment.

title: Pre-processing workflow
section: What to check before downstream analysis
text:
What to check before downstream analysis
Before opening Overview or DEP analysis, verify that sample names match sample_info, no sample is unexpectedly all missing, transformed values are on the intended scale, imputation did not create implausible distributions, and normalization reduced unwanted sample-level shifts without erasing known biological differences.

title: Data transformation
text:
The current transformation menu provides:

None
log10
log2
Standardization
Z-Score
scale
center
scale-center

Choose a method that matches the scale and distribution of the imported quantitative data. Do not log-transform values that are already on a logarithmic scale.

scale

title: Data transformation
text:
GUI workflow

Click Load data. ProtVis uses the active ProtVis_dataset first and can recover Step3_correct_noise.rda for legacy projects.
Inspect the Original Data table and visualization.
Select a Transformation Method.
Click Run transformation.
Compare the Transformed Data and its boxplot with the original distribution.
Adjust the plot colors only for presentation; color settings do not alter the quantitative matrix.
Download original/transformed plots as PDF when needed.

title: Data transformation
text:
Choosing a transformation
For many intensity-based proteomics datasets, log2 is useful when values are positive and strongly right-skewed. Standardization or Z-score transformations are useful for pattern-oriented visualization but change the meaning of absolute differences, so the intended downstream model should guide the choice.






Warning



Log transformations require valid positive values. Missing measurements should remain NA; do not replace them with arbitrary constants merely to make a log transform succeed.

title: Data transformation
text:
Output
The transformed state is written to the ProtVis_dataset and the compatibility file:
Step4_data_transformed.rda
Continue with Data imputation.

title: Background make
text: Background Make converts eggNOG-mapper-style annotation into the background workbook required by the Enrichment Analysis module.

title: Background make
text: Background Make converts eggNOG-mapper-style annotation into the background workbook required by the Enrichment Analysis module.

title: Background make
text:
Required annotation fields
Upload the eggNOG output in .csv or .xlsx format. The module checks for:

query
GOs
KEGG_Pathway

title: Background make
text:
Protein/transcript separator
Set the separator used to reduce transcript-level IDs to the desired protein/gene identifier. For example, with:
Zm00001eb321680_T001
using _ extracts:
Zm00001eb321680
Only apply this rule if it matches the identifier convention of your study.

title: Background make
text:
Generate the workbook

Upload the eggNOG annotation.
Click Check File.
Set the ID separator.
Click Make Background.
Review the generated GO and KEGG tables.
Download the Excel workbook.

The enrichment-ready workbook contains:
GO_background
KEGG_background
and each sheet should provide the TERM, GENE, and NAME fields expected by the current Enrichment Analysis file validator.






Important



Build the background from the set of proteins that could realistically have been detected/tested in the experiment, not from the list of significant proteins. The background defines the enrichment universe.

title: Toolkits
text:
Toolkits are intentionally smaller than the core pipeline. They help prepare identifiers/annotations, inspect proteins, generate focused plots, or connect results to external resources.
Current utilities include Protein Extract, Background Make, Protein Links, Protein Structure, Boxplot, SwissModel, STRINGdb PPI, Stacked Column Diagram, Correlation chord, and DEG Analyse.

title: Toolkits
text:
Toolkits are intentionally smaller than the core pipeline. They help prepare identifiers/annotations, inspect proteins, generate focused plots, or connect results to external resources.
Current utilities include Protein Extract, Background Make, Protein Links, Protein Structure, Boxplot, SwissModel, STRINGdb PPI, Stacked Column Diagram, Correlation chord, and DEG Analyse.

title: Toolkits
text:
How to use toolkits responsibly

Keep the input table used by the toolkit together with the exported figure.
Use stable protein/gene identifiers when moving between ProtVis and external databases.
Record species/taxonomy settings for database-backed tools.
Treat structure and network visualizations as evidence-supporting views, not automatic proof of mechanism.
Prefer the main workflow’s ProtVis_dataset results as the source of quantitative values rather than manually retyping numbers.

The sidebar provides dedicated pages for the most commonly used utilities.

title: Correlation chord
text: A correlation chord diagram is useful for a filtered subset of relationships among proteins, traits, pathways, metabolites or other variables. It becomes difficult to interpret when every possible pair is displayed.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Recommended workflow

Start from a numeric matrix or correlation table with stable variable names.
Choose the correlation method appropriate to the data.
Apply an effect-size threshold and, when available, a significance criterion.
Keep only biologically relevant relationships.
Draw the chord diagram and inspect whether line width/color encodes the intended statistic.
Export the filtered edge table used to generate the plot.







Warning



Correlation does not establish causation. For high-dimensional correlation screens, p-values also require attention to multiple testing and non-independence among features.

title: Protein structure
text: The Protein Structure toolkit helps move from a candidate protein identifier or structure file to a three-dimensional view. ProtVis includes structure-related dependencies such as bio3d and r3dmol, and also exposes a SwissModel-oriented utility in the Toolkits menu.

title: Protein structure
text: The Protein Structure toolkit helps move from a candidate protein identifier or structure file to a three-dimensional view. ProtVis includes structure-related dependencies such as bio3d and r3dmol, and also exposes a SwissModel-oriented utility in the Toolkits menu.

title: Protein structure
text:
Recommended workflow

Resolve the candidate to a stable protein identifier.
Obtain or upload the structure format expected by the selected toolkit.
Confirm chain/residue numbering before mapping a mutation, PTM or domain of interest.
Generate the interactive or static structural view.
Record the structure source and model/entry identifier in the figure legend or Methods.







Warning



Predicted structures and experimental structures are not equivalent evidence. When using a model, report its source and confidence/quality metrics and avoid over-interpreting poorly supported regions.

title: Boxplot
text: Upload an .xlsx table in wide format, with one quantitative group per column. The module uses the column names as group labels.

title: Boxplot
text:
Workflow

Upload the Excel file.
Select the groups to display.
Choose pairwise comparisons.
Set x- and y-axis labels.
Customize group colors, box width, point size and outline color.
Choose a ggplot theme.
Review the statistical annotations.
Set output width/height and download the figure as PDF.

The current boxplot workflow uses pairwise t-tests via ggpubr::stat_compare_means.






Important



A t-test assumes an appropriate design and distributional model. Do not apply independent pairwise t-tests to paired/repeated-measures data without accounting for pairing, and consider multiple-testing correction when many comparisons are shown.

title: Data input
text:
The Data input page is selected dynamically from the source chosen during Project init. Its job is to load the source-specific quantitative evidence, remove unreliable entries where appropriate, and hand a clean expression matrix to preprocessing.
ProtVis currently routes the following source types to dedicated or parser-backed modules: Raw, MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, Mascot, OpenMS, and User-defined matrix.

title: Data input
text:
Recommended workflow

Complete Project init first.
Open Data input and confirm that the header shows the expected source.
Load the corresponding search-engine/export file if the selected source requires one.
Review the raw/source preview before filtering.
Apply the source-specific unreliable-evidence filtering controls.
Confirm that the output retains a protein identifier and the expected samples.
Continue to Pre-processing → Correct Noise.

title: Data input
text:
Source-specific behavior
Different proteomics tools use different column names and evidence flags. ProtVis therefore avoids forcing every source through a MaxQuant-only parser. Parser-backed sources are converted into a common protein-by-sample representation before they enter the shared workflow.
For MaxQuant-style inputs, common unreliable records include reverse hits, contaminants, and entries flagged as identified only by site. Other sources use their own available evidence fields.






WarningDo not treat zeros or sentinel values as biological abundance



Missing or not-observed measurements must remain missing until the explicit imputation stage. In the current workflow, values such as 0 and the legacy -8 sentinel are converted to NA before imputation where applicable.

title: Data input
text:
Built-in source fixtures
ProtVis ships small examples for several input ecosystems, including MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, OpenMS, and mzTab-oriented data. These fixtures are useful for verifying that a parser is operational.
A programmatic example is:
library(ProtVis)

example_data <- load_protvis_builtin_data(
  source = "DIA-NN",
  auto_export = FALSE
)

example_data

title: Data input
text:
Output and compatibility
Current modules update the canonical ProtVis_dataset. The GUI also maintains stage snapshots used by downstream compatibility paths. Correct Noise can recover the imported stage from Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda when an in-memory ProtVis_dataset is not available.
The preferred workflow is to keep the active ProtVis_dataset intact rather than manually opening, modifying, and resaving stage .rda files.
